Q: wmic os get localdatetime suddenly failing A:

Seems dt is empty for some reason. You still can request WMI through VBS.

NOTE: VBS still may be depricated in the future: https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/windows-itpro-blog/vbscript-deprecation-timelines-and-next-steps/4148301

NOTE: The WMIC is not WMI.

Source code
  • wmi/print_wmi_local_datetime.vbs
  • wmi/get_wmi_local_datetime.vbs.bat

print_wmi_local_datetime.vbs:

Dim objWMI : Set objWMI = GetObject("winmgmts:")
Dim objSet: Set objSet = objWMI.InstancesOf("Win32_OperatingSystem")

Dim obj
For Each obj in objSet
    WScript.Echo obj.LocalDateTime
    Exit For
Next

get_wmi_local_datetime.vbs.bat:

@echo off

rem drop return value
set "RETURN_VALUE="

rem CAUTION:
rem   `for /F` does not return a command error code
for /F "usebackq tokens=* delims="eol^= %%i in (`@"%%SystemRoot%%\System32\cscript.exe" //nologo "%~dp0print_wmi_local_datetime.vbs" 2^>nul`) do set "RETURN_VALUE=%%i"

if defined RETURN_VALUE endlocal & set "RETURN_VALUE=%RETURN_VALUE:~0,18%" & exit /b 0

exit /b 1

rem Description:
rem   Independent to Windows locale date/time request.

Q: Convert string in iso8601 format to datetime A:

Note, that ISO 8601 permits many formats.

x <- c(
  ## time precision (with offset)
  "2026-04-02T02-04:40",
  "2026-04-02T02:16-04:40",
  "2026-04-02T02:16:01-04:40",
  
  ## fractional seconds
  "2026-04-02T02:16:01.5-04:40",
  "2026-04-02T02:16:01.123456-04:40",
  
  ## UTC designator
  "2026-04-02T06:16Z",
  "2026-04-02T06:16:01Z",
  
  ## compact (basic format)
  "20260402T0216-0440",
  "20260402T021601-0440",
  
  ## date only
  "2026-04-02",
  
  ## week date
  "2026-W14-4",
  
  ## ordinal date
  "2026-092",
  
  ## edge cases
  "2026-04-02T02:16",
  "2026-04-02T02:16:01.123Z"
)

parsedate::parse_iso_8601() appears to handle this set correctly.

> parsedate::parse_date(x)
 [1] "2026-04-02 06:40:00 UTC"
 [2] "2026-04-02 06:56:00 UTC"
 [3] "2026-04-02 06:56:01 UTC"
 [4] "2026-04-02 06:56:01 UTC"
 [5] "2026-04-02 06:56:01 UTC"
 [6] "2026-04-02 06:16:00 UTC"
 [7] "2026-04-02 06:16:01 UTC"
 [8] "2026-04-02 06:56:00 UTC"
 [9] "2026-04-02 06:56:01 UTC"
[10] "2026-04-02 00:00:00 UTC"
[11] "2026-04-02 00:00:00 UTC"
[12] "2026-04-02 00:00:00 UTC"
[13] "2026-04-02 02:16:00 UTC"
[14] "2026-04-02 02:16:01 UTC"

Missing components are imputed, and naive times are interpreted in the system timezone.

Caveat: very flexible, but much slower (~3–40× here; parsedate 1.3.2; R 4.5.3).

> n <- 1e5
> x1 <- x[sample.int(length(x), n, replace=TRUE)]
> x2 <- sample.int(n, n) |> as.POSIXct() |> as.character()
> microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
+   parse_iso_8601=parsedate::parse_iso_8601(x1),
+   readr=readr::parse_datetime(x1),
+   iso8601=iso8601::iso8601todatetime(x1),
+   strptime=strptime(x2, '%F %T'),  ## fixed format, not ISO
+   times=3L
+ ) |> suppressWarnings() |> suppressMessages()

Q: Pyinstaller throws a syntax error when I try to use it A:

PyInstaller is a command-line tool, not something you call like a normal Python function.

You're getting a syntax error because this is not valid Python:

pyinstaller "C:\Python\w3\factorial_play.py"

Run it from the terminal/command prompt instead:

pyinstaller C:\Python\w3\factorial_play.py

If pyinstaller is not on PATH, use:

python -m PyInstaller C:\Python\w3\factorial_play.py

That works without changing PATH.

Q: How does Costco avoid having to use Apple In App Purchase A:

This mainly comes down to how Apple classifies the service.

If the membership is tied to real-world access or benefits (like shopping in-store, warehouse entry, etc.), Apple usually allows external payment methods because the value isn’t consumed purely inside the app. That’s why companies like Costco can handle memberships outside of in-app purchases.

But if your app is offering purely digital content or features, then Apple typically requires you to use their in-app purchase system and take their cut.

It’s less about the business model and more about where the value is actually delivered—inside the app vs. outside in the real world.

I was looking into this while researching Costco’s app features and membership flow, and found this breakdown useful:
👉 https://faisalmian.com/does-costco-have-scan-and-go-checkout/

Might give you a clearer idea of how they structure things 👍

Q: How to Construct the Pattern for a REXEXP_SUBSTR in Oracle sql developer A:

Not very familiar with Oracle regex functions but from a cursory glance REGEXP_REPLACE should make it easier. Make a pattern that matches the whole input while capturing the two parts you're interested in into capturing groups, and replace by a string containing references to the two groups. For instance,

SELECT REGEXP_REPLACE(sourceColumnOrExpr, '^blah blah blah (\w+) yada yada (\w+) da-da-da$', '\1 \2') FROM sourceTable;

I've used \w+ as wildcard for what you're trying to match, replace with whatever is appropriate but try to be specific (avoid .*) to prevent bad performances.

Q: Is there a cheap way to wait and wake threads in Java? A:

If you really want to have low latency, don't weak up any threads. Just spin. This will cost you a few cores, but it will give you orders of magnitude better latency.

Q: Should XRef stream offset be always stored, in that very stream or any other? A:

The PDF specification clearly says:

Like any stream, a cross-reference stream shall be an indirect object. Therefore, an entry for it shall exist in either a cross-reference stream (usually itself) or in a cross-reference table (in hybridreference files

(ISO 32000-2, section 7.5.8.3)

Thus, the construct you show strictly speaking is invalid.

That being said, one again and again finds PDFs with this kind of error and most PDF processors usually don't even realize it.

Nonetheless, one should definitively avoid such errors because in certain contexts they may suddenly cause issues. E.g. errors in cross reference tables are known to cause validation errors in PDFs with multiple signatures in Adobe Acrobat.
